team.name: flaxos
team.notes: Keen to keep things grounded, iterate with coding agents, and ensure we actually ship a playable build.

team.name: Scotty
team.notes: Ready to pair on multiplayer mechanics and co-op shenanigans.

questions.title: What is our hard deadline for Milestone 1 (First Playable Build)?
questions.subtitle: The #1 reason agentic game dev projects stall is indefinite timelines. We need a rapid, locked-in target for 2 players to connect and play.

options.title: The 48-Hour Weekend Jam Sprint
options.description: Hyper-focused 2-day hackathon. Graybox circles, simple sync, 1 mechanic. Playable by Sunday night.
options.caution: High intensity over a single weekend.

options.title: The 2-Week Vertical Slice (Recommended)
options.description: 14 days from kickoff to playable squad playtest. 1 arena, 2 character classes, core win/loss loop.
pros: Allows polish on core combat feel
options.caution: Requires holding each other strictly accountable each week.

options.title: The 1-Month Milestone
options.description: 4 structured weekly sprints. Deeper architectural foundations, sound effects, full lobby flow.
pros: More breathing room for complex netcode
options.caution: Higher risk of enthusiasm tapering off if week 1 doesn't produce something moving on screen.

comments.text: I really want us to have something we can physically play together within 2 weeks max. Once we play together, the momentum is unstoppable!

questions.title: Which Anti-Abandonment Rule will be our sacred team covenant?
questions.subtitle: To overcome the curse of unfinished game dev projects, we must agree on our guiding constraint.

options.title: The 'Graybox First' Covenant
options.description: Zero custom art, sound, or complex menus until two actual human players can move, shoot/interact, and score in a graybox arena.
pros: Proves fun before spending time on art
options.caution: Looks ugly for the first 3 days, but feels amazing when it works.

options.title: The 'Friday 8pm Playtest Night' Covenant
options.description: Every Friday at 8:00 PM we hop on Discord and play whatever build exists. No excuses. If it crashes, we laugh and fix it live.
pros: Makes game dev a social event
options.caution: Requires reserving the Friday evening slot.

options.title: The 'Rule of One Core Mechanic'
options.description: v0.1 has only ONE primary verb (e.g. either dashing, or shooting, or grappling). We only add a second verb after the first is 10/10 juicy.
options.caution: Requires discipline to resist adding 'wouldn't it be cool if...' features.

questions.title: What genre & core gameplay loop should we build?
questions.subtitle: Needs to be inherently fun in co-op/multiplayer and achievable with agentic AI pair programming.

options.title: Co-op Horde Survival (Vampire Survivors × Risk of Rain)
options.description: 2-4 players hold out in dynamic arenas against swarming waves. Shared XP gems, synergized elemental upgrades, clutch revive beacons.
pros: Low netcode overhead (enemies can use deterministic swarming)
Easy to add tons of fun agent-generated weapons
options.caution: Screen can get busy if weapon particles aren't disciplined.

options.title: Top-Down Extraction / Micro-Raid (Zero Sievert × Enter the Gungeon)
options.description: Fast 8-10 minute raids into hostile derelict sectors. Scavenge tech components, fight rogue AI drones, rush to extraction beacon before meltdown.
pros: Natural meta-progression in the ship hub
options.caution: Requires inventory sync and extract logic.

options.title: Chaotic Physics Arena Brawler (Duck Game × Rounds × Stick Fight)
options.description: Fast, goofy 1-minute rounds. Physics-driven knockback, bizarre randomized weapon drops, destructible platforms, sudden death.
options.caution: Physics sync over high ping can be tricky if not client-authoritative with rollback.

options.title: Twin-Stick Co-op Dungeon Crawler / ARPG
options.description: Procedural rooms, dodge-roll combat, telegraph attacks, combo abilities, and coordinated boss fights with distinct phases.
options.caution: Requires more enemy AI states and room generator logic.

options.title: Space Station Subterfuge / Social Deception (SS13-lite)
options.description: Keep a rickety space expedition vessel running with mini-tasks while random malfunctions (or a secret rogue saboteur) cause chaos.
options.caution: Requires at least 4-5 players to shine.

comments.text: Horde survival or extraction both sound super fun. With horde survival, even 2 of us can jump in and have a blast immediately without needing a full lobby.

questions.title: What engine & tech stack should power the game?
questions.subtitle: The engine dictates how quickly our AI agents can write code, how fast we can test, and how easy it is for friends to join.

options.title: Godot 4.x (GDScript)
options.description: Lightweight, blazing fast launch times, clean text-based scene files that git merges seamlessly, and LLMs write top-tier GDScript.
options.caution: Requires downloading Godot 4 editor (though lightweight ~100MB).

options.title: Web-Native (TypeScript + Phaser 3 / Pixi.js / Three.js + Vite)
options.description: Zero installation barrier. Send a URL link in Discord or WhatsApp, click it, and all friends are playing together in Chrome/Firefox in 3 seconds.
pros: Absolute zero friction for playtesting with friends
options.caution: Browser audio/fullscreen quirks; requires web netcode (WebSocket/WebRTC).

options.title: Godot 4.x (C# / .NET)
options.description: Full Godot engine capabilities with strict static typing, LINQ, and familiar C# architecture.
pros: Strong types prevent silly runtime bugs
options.caution: Slightly heavier build step than pure GDScript.

options.title: Bevy (Rust ECS)
options.description: Modern data-driven Entity Component System in Rust. Blazing fast, pure code, zero graphical editor required.
options.caution: Rust compile times can slow down rapid agentic iterations.

questions.title: What multiplayer architecture & networking model should we use?
questions.subtitle: Complex netcode kills indie projects. We must choose the simplest path that delivers snappy, lag-free fun.

options.title: Authoritative WebSocket / Node.js Server (Colyseus or Custom Room State)
options.description: Fast Node.js / TypeScript room server running a 30Hz or 60Hz tick loop with client-side interpolation. Clients send inputs, server sends world snapshots.
pros: Easy to run locally or host on a $5 VPS / Render / Fly.io
Both Web and Desktop clients can connect
options.caution: Requires hosting or running a local server terminal.

options.title: Steamworks P2P Lobby (Steam P2P / Godot ENet)
options.description: Host player acts as listen-server. Friends join via Steam overlay or room code with automatic NAT punch-through.
options.caution: Requires Steam running and a Steam App ID (or Spacewar 480 test ID).

options.title: Local Shared Screen / Steam Remote Play Together
options.description: v0.1 is built as a single-screen local co-op game. Friends connect via Steam Remote Play or Parsec or Discord screen-share with zero netcode!
pros: Can add real netcode in Milestone 2
options.caution: Requires host bandwidth and game must support shared screen or splitscreen.

options.title: WebRTC DataChannels (Peer-to-Peer Browser Mesh)
options.description: Direct browser-to-browser UDP-like connections using WebRTC DataChannels for ultra-low latency.
pros: No central server relaying gameplay ticks
options.caution: Signaling and STUN/TURN server setup needed.

comments.text: Authoritative WebSocket room server is awesome because we can write it in TypeScript/Node with full test coverage, and agents write great server tick loops!

questions.title: What visual direction & art style should we target?
questions.subtitle: Art must look distinctive and cohesive without becoming an asset creation bottleneck that halts development.

options.title: 16-Bit Crisp Pixel Art (Retro Sci-Fi)
options.description: Chunky 32x32 sprites, vibrant palette, expressive walk cycles, dynamic lighting on top of 2D tiles.
pros: Easy for agents to generate matching sprites
options.caution: Can feel generic if palette and juice (screenshake, particles) aren't dialed in.

options.title: Stylized Low-Poly 3D / Retro PS1 Crunch
options.description: Flat-shaded low polygon meshes with vertex coloring or crunchy low-res textures, dramatic point lights, modern post-processing.
pros: Very trendy indie aesthetic (Lethal Company / Ultrakill vibe)
Easy to prototype with geometric primitives in 3D
options.caution: Requires 3D math and camera handling.

options.title: Minimalist Neon Vector / Synthwave Geometry
options.description: Glowing geometric wireframes, particle blooms, dark space backgrounds, synthwave color bursts (cyan, magenta, electric yellow).
pros: Focus 100% on gameplay feel, juicy particles, and lighting
options.caution: Less character personality compared to sprites.

options.title: Isometric 2.5D (HD-2D style)
options.description: Layered isometric perspective with pixel characters, dynamic cast shadows, and depth-sorted terrain.
options.caution: Isometric depth sorting and collision math can be fiddly.

questions.title: Which core mechanics will make our game uniquely addictive?
questions.subtitle: Select up to 3 core mechanics that create memorable multiplayer moments and emergent chaos. (Multi-select enabled)

options.title: Synergistic Elemental Combos (Spell / Tech Fusing)
options.description: Player A lays down a Cryo Field or Oil Slick, Player B fires Lightning or Plasma into it to cause an Overload explosion. Teammates must coordinate!
options.caution: Needs clear status effect rules.

options.title: Physics Havoc & Hilarious Ragdolls / Knockback
options.description: Shockwaves knock enemies into environmental hazard pits, explosive barrels chain-react, bouncy shields reflect lasers.
pros: Emergent gameplay without complex scripted events
options.caution: Ensure friendly knockback is fun, not grief-inducing.

options.title: Shared 'Discovery Super' Meter
options.description: The squad shares one giant energy gauge. When maxed, both players must simultaneously hit a button to trigger an epic screen-clearing super weapon.
options.caution: Needs clear visual HUD indicator.

options.title: Unstable Sector Hazards & Escaping Collapse
options.description: Solar flares disable shields, containment leaks flood sectors with radiation, extraction zone changes location dynamically.
options.caution: Hazards must be clearly telegraphed to feel fair.

options.title: Asymmetric Roles (e.g. Breacher vs Tech Specialist)
options.description: One player wields heavy ordnance and shields; the other operates remote drones, hacks terminal doors, and calls in supply drops.
options.caution: Both roles must feel equally thrilling to play.

options.title: Clutch Defibrillator & Friendly Revive Dome
options.description: When a teammate goes down, they enter a crawling beacon state. A surviving player can deploy a temporary shield dome to channel a 4-second revive.
options.caution: Revive dome needs a long cooldown so it cannot be spammed

comments.text: Combining abilities (like cryo + lightning) makes co-op feel like real teamwork instead of just two people shooting in parallel!

questions.title: What lore & narrative vibe fits 'Team Discovery Channel' best?
questions.subtitle: Gives personality to our characters, weapons, voice barks, and interface.

options.title: Team Discovery: Derelict Deep Space Expeditions
options.description: A ragtag salvage science crew exploring abandoned megastructures on the galactic rim. Retro CRT terminals, malfunctioning research AI, cosmic oddities.
pros: Justifies weird experimental weapons and alien artifacts
Great blend of wonder and danger
options.caution: None, it's a stellar fit.

options.title: Corporate Dystopia / Intergalactic Custodians
options.description: Overworked space station janitors battling sentient bureaucracy mutants with high-powered mop-cannons and recycling beamers.
options.caution: Humor can be subjective.

options.title: Cyberpunk Data Heist
options.description: Infiltrate neon data vaults, crack corporate ICE, extract digital payloads while fighting digital enforcers.
options.caution: Cyberpunk is a well-trodden indie space.

questions.title: How should we divide the core development pillars?
questions.subtitle: Clear ownership prevents bystander effect. Everyone has an assigned domain while pairing with AI agents.

options.title: AI Agent Orchestrator & Prompt Architect
options.description: Owns the system prompts, architectural rules, agent dev loop (Codex/Antigravity/Claude Code), and keeping code structure clean.
pros: Ensures agents don't produce spaghetti code
options.caution: Must maintain clean documentation and types.

options.title: Multiplayer Netcode & Lobby Czar
options.description: Owns room management, player connection state, snapshot serialization, and latency compensation.
pros: Single owner for the most delicate system
options.caution: High responsibility to keep the sync bug-free.

options.title: Combat Feel & Juice Lead (Screen Shake, Controls, Hitstop)
options.description: Tunes weapon recoil, dodge roll responsiveness, sound triggers, impact effects, and damage numbers.
pros: Directly makes the game addictive to play
Super fun domain to iterate on
options.caution: Requires lots of playtesting tweaks.

options.title: Weapons, Perks & Enemy Scripter
options.description: Designs and scripts new enemy attack patterns, synergy perks, boss phases, and level spawn tables using AI prompts.
pros: Fast to prompt with AI agents once foundation is set
options.caution: Keep balance within sane bounds.

options.title: QA, DevOps & Friday Playtest Host
options.description: Ensures the build compiles, runs playtest servers on Friday night, records bug tickets, and keeps the team celebrated.
pros: The heartbeat that keeps the squad motivated and shipping
options.caution: Must be organized and consistent.

comments.text: I can lead the AI agent tooling/prompt architecture and QA builds, while Scotty and I pair on netcode and juicy combat mechanics!
